column3: Contrasts Allah's command with a hostile command toward evil and unsupported speech about Him.
The divided-servant parable sharply contrasts many rival masters with undivided belonging to one.
Explicitly withholds final decision over repentance and punishment from the messenger.
Concerns deceptive oaths and their consequences, without clarifying the focus claim.
Directly denies that one given Book, judgment, and prophethood could claim human servants besides Allah.
Shows an affair bearing consequences, but does not identify human or angelic religious authority.
Direct parallel: worship Allah alone and do not take one another as lords besides Him.
Locates Abraham in surrender and apart from association, supporting the closing appeal to being Muslim.
Angels administering an affair suggests delegated activity, not delegated lordship.
Names religious scholars, monks, and the Messiah being taken as lords, against worship of one God.
States divine forgiveness and mercy without adding to the authority question.
Its settled affair is too general to distinguish legitimate from illegitimate command.
Allah commands trust restitution and just judgment, marking His command as the norm for human judgment.
Divine favor is selective, but the verse does not address assigning lordship to intermediaries.
States that the whole affair belongs to Allah despite human assumptions of control.
The Messiah and near angels are servants of Allah, directly resisting their elevation to lordship.
States the painful punishment without adding to the focus.
Obedience to what Allah commands supports divine normativity but is distant from the focus's agents.
A claimed faith that commands disobedience is exposed as corrupt, paralleling the test of a command's source.
Affiliation with Abraham is framed through following and belief, not through elevated human lordship.
A decreed affair displays divine determination but does not concern rival religious authority.
Forbids taking disbelievers as protective authorities over believers, a related boundary of allegiance.
Guidance and favor are placed in Allah's hand rather than a group's control.
Commends patience and forgiveness but does not materially illuminate the focus.
Limits familial allegiance when it prefers disbelief, preserving loyalty against rival claims.
The clear Book is given, but no authority relation is specified.
Shared work in Moses's affair shows assistance can be delegated without making the helper a lord.
Moses relays Allah's command rather than issuing an independent sacred demand.
The messenger is commanded to worship the Lord alone and to be among those who surrender.
Allah's command is one and immediate, reinforcing a single undivided ultimate authority.
Revelation centers one God and asks whether hearers will surrender, closely matching 3:80's conclusion.
Worship is directed to Allah alone with no association, even within promised communal authority.
Angels convey the command from Allah to servants; transmission does not divide its source or deity.
The revealed knowledge belongs to Allah and its conclusion is exclusive deity and surrender.
Describes the wise Book but contributes no explicit authority boundary.
Contrasts Allah's completed command with human failure to fulfill what was commanded.
Angelic support is granted by the Lord in answer to prayer, presenting angels as aids rather than lords.
The Lord of all realms alone is to be worshiped; no namesake or equal is admitted.
Allah's command overturns apparent human control, but the link to angelic or prophetic lordship is indirect.
The inherited worship commitment is to one God, with surrender directed to Him.
Angels descend only by the Lord's command and within His encompassing possession.
A command to reverence is relevant to moral direction, but does not resolve the focus's authority boundary.
Warns against a competing network of loyalties, a secondary parallel to rejecting rival religious authority.
All affairs return to Allah; worship and reliance therefore remain directed to Him.
A human's coercive command exposes an illegitimate rival demand, contrary to the focus's divine command.
The angels' collective prostration displays their obedience, not an entitlement to worship.
Allah addresses angels as creatures in the creation scene, supporting their subordinate status.
Kingship is Allah's and all affairs return to Him, grounding ultimate authority in Him alone.
Angelic reinforcement comes from the believers' Lord, preserving Allah as the source behind angelic aid.
The objection to following one human records a dispute but does not itself clarify proper authority.
Explicitly forbids obeying the command of transgressors, so not every command merits obedience.
Places disbelief after faith under grave judgment, supporting 3:80's warning about being commanded to disbelief.
The Book given to Moses as guidance supports prophetic reception, not prophetic lordship.
Calls the ruling Allah's command sent down, but its domestic application is only a remote parallel.
Joins belief in Allah, angels, Book, and prophets without confusing their distinct places.
Allah's decisive command brings creation into being directly, emphasizing His unique effective authority.
Prohibits treating Allah's signs as mockery, but does not address elevating intermediaries.
All affairs return to Allah while He knows those before and behind them, retaining ultimate ownership.
Disbelief disqualifies idolaters from maintaining Allah's mosques, linking worship space to right allegiance.
Submitting one's face to Allah leads to the firm hold, while the outcome of affairs returns to Him.
Angels carry a sign of kingship, showing service in a sign without making them objects of worship.
A wise affair is differentiated, but no human or angelic authority relation is stated.
Regulates testimony in a bequest and offers no focused contribution.
Even empowered believers order good and forbid wrong, while the final outcome remains Allah's.
Affirms revelation to many prophets while refusing distinctions among them and directing surrender to Allah.
A communicated decree shows prophetic reception of a fixed affair, not prophetic ultimate authority.
Concerns concealed disbelief, without a meaningful link to the focus.
The Spirit is from the Lord's command and human knowledge is limited, preserving the command's divine source.
Depicts later mutual blame between the weak and arrogant, only indirectly concerning misplaced human influence.
Shows a false authority issuing commands that distort Allah's creation; taking it as patron is declared loss.
Places the messenger within a continuous chain of recipients of revelation, supporting reception rather than self-originated lordship.
Allah's command carries His will into existence, a high contrast with creaturely authority.
Marks an irreconcilable distinction between worship directed by the messenger and the opponents' worship.
No partner is admitted, and the messenger's commanded response is to be first among those who surrender.
A prophet mediates the people's request and challenges their resolve, but the verse does not elevate him as lord.
Competing love and waiting for Allah's affair are relevant to loyalty, but not directly to divine delegation.
Rejects calling on what cannot benefit or harm and commands surrender to the Lord of all worlds.
Questions whether their own minds command this, exposing an alternative and unreliable source of direction.
Commands continued calling to the Lord and rejection of association after the signs are received.
A human commands household prayer while Allah alone provides, distinguishing service from sovereign provision.
Concerns oaths and reconciliation, without a clear contribution to the focus.
The messenger publicly delivers what he is commanded, presenting him as commissioned rather than sovereign.
The messenger calls people to faith in their Lord under a prior covenant, not to faith in himself.
Once Allah and His messenger decide an affair, believers cannot reopen it as their own option; the messenger's authority is joined to Allah's decision.
Describes limited harm and failed opposition, without bearing on lordship or command.
Obedience and truthful action are demanded when an affair becomes firm, but the source is not explicit.
Sets Satan's command toward indecency against Allah's promise, contrasting rival moral direction.
Refusal to prostrate at a command is portrayed as growing aversion to the One addressed as the Merciful.
Rebukes disbelief in Allah's signs despite witnessing them, supporting the warning against departure from submission.
Allah's path is the path of the One who owns all realms, and all affairs move toward Him.
Angels' descent at the final event is relevant only as a scene of their creaturely appearance.
A fighting party must return to Allah's command, making communal correction answer to a higher authority.
Its detailed just order shows instruction in human dealings, but adds little on angels or prophets as lords.
Angels do not disobey Allah's commands and do what they are commanded, explicitly portraying them as obedient servants.
Questions worship of what cannot hear, see, or benefit, directly challenging misplaced worship.
A father's command to prayer and good is framed as ethical counsel, a limited human role rather than lordship.
Allah's direct command and prohibition to Adam establish the divine boundary whose violation is wrongdoing.
Leaders guide by Allah's command, making their leadership derivative rather than its source.
Testing striving and patience does not clarify the focus's authority relations.
A command addressed through the Prophet regulates conduct, but the focus link is only the Prophet's commissioned role.
Allah's exclusive living sovereignty and permission-bound intercession rule out autonomous sacred authority.
Rejecting false authorities is paired with belief in Allah, clarifying the allegiance implied by surrender.
Belief includes Allah, angels, Books, and messengers without collapsing these distinct roles into deity.
Allah, the angels, and those given knowledge testify to one deity, keeping angels as witnesses rather than lords.
Jesus directs worship to Allah as his Lord and theirs, directly excluding his own deification.
Affirms that there is no deity except Allah and identifies Him as the Mighty and Wise.
Commands worship of Allah and association of nothing with Him, the central boundary stated in 3:80.
Declares association with Allah unforgiven unless He wills otherwise, intensifying the focus's rejection of it.
Repeats the gravity of associating partners with Allah and its departure from the right way.
Names the Messiah a messenger and word from Allah while forbidding elevation through excess in religion.
The Messiah calls for worship of Allah, his Lord and theirs, while association is explicitly barred.
Rejects dividing deity into three and reasserts one God.
Depicts the Messiah and his mother as dependent humans, countering their treatment as lords.
Denies that anything besides Allah possesses power over harm or benefit.
The Messiah disavows calling people to take him and his mother as gods besides Allah.
Condemns making jinn partners of Allah despite His creating them.
Identifies Allah as creator of all things and commands worship of Him alone.
Commands following revealed truth and turning away from those who associate partners.
Rejects seeking any lord other than Allah, who is Lord of all things.
Creation and command both belong to Allah, grounding His unique governing authority.
A messenger calls his people to worship Allah alone, showing the prophetic role as summons to Allah.
Challenges invocation of powerless others and their alleged intercessory role before Allah.
The messenger refuses worship of what others worship and directs worship to Allah alone.
Forbids calling on what neither benefits nor harms apart from Allah.
Judgment belongs only to Allah, who commands worship of none but Him.
Allah is identified as Lord and creator while alleged partners are challenged as powerless.
The messenger is commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him.
Every community receives the same call: worship Allah and avoid false authorities.
Forbids taking two gods and identifies Allah as the one God to be feared.
The Lord decrees worship of none but Him, a direct command of exclusive devotion.
Those called besides Allah lack power to remove harm or alter it.
Condemns taking Allah's servants as protectors besides Him, directly relevant to elevating creatures.
Requires worship of one God and forbids associating anyone in worship of the Lord.
Jesus identifies himself as Allah's servant and recipient of the Book and prophethood.
Jesus declares Allah his Lord and their Lord and calls for His worship.
Taking gods besides Allah for honor exposes the misplaced elevation of false objects of worship.
Allah commands worship of Himself alone.
Aaron calls his people to worship the Most Merciful and follow him as a messenger.
Every messenger receives the same revelation: there is no deity but Allah, so worship Him.
Those called Allah's children are instead honored servants, resisting creaturely elevation.
Any creature claiming deity besides Allah is assigned the consequence of that false claim.
Allah alone is the True, while what is called besides Him is false.
Those invoked besides Allah cannot create even a fly and cannot reclaim what it takes.
Allah has no child and no other deity with Him; rival gods would contend over creation.
Those taken besides Allah neither create nor control death, life, or resurrection.
Abraham commands his people to worship Allah and be mindful of Him.
What is worshiped besides Allah cannot provide; provision is to be sought from Allah and worship directed to Him.
Those called besides Allah possess no atom's weight in the heavens or earth and share no ownership.
Allah asks the angels whether people had worshiped them, distinguishing angels from objects of worship.
The angels disavow such worship and identify Allah as their protector.
Allah is named the sole creator and provider; no deity exists except Him.
Allah's covenant commands humanity not to worship Satan and to worship Him on a straight path.
Sincere religion belongs to Allah, while claimed intermediaries are exposed as a rival devotional rationale.
All intercession belongs to Allah, denying independent sacred brokerage.
Allah is creator of all things and disposer over them, grounding exclusive authority.
The messenger refuses any command to worship other than Allah.
Associating partners when Allah is invoked reveals the rejection of His exclusive deity.
Abraham dissociates himself from what his people worship apart from the Creator.
The messengers before the Prophet provide a test against any claim that gods besides the Merciful were authorized.
The Messiah is described as a servant favored by Allah, not as a lord.
Jesus calls for worship of Allah as his Lord and theirs, identifying the straight path.
Challenges alleged partners to show any created share or scriptural warrant for their authority.
Forbids positing another god with Allah.
Even angels cannot intercede except after Allah permits and accepts, excluding autonomous angelic authority.
Places places of worship exclusively for Allah and forbids calling anyone alongside Him.
The messenger calls upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
The messenger denies possessing independent power to harm or guide, limiting creaturely authority.
Commands sincere worship of Allah, upright devotion, prayer, and almsgiving.
Declares Allah uniquely one.
Declares Allah the self-sufficient refuge, excluding creaturely dependence as divine status.
Denies divine begetting or being begotten, countering familial elevation of creatures.
Denies that anything is comparable to Allah.
